blocks.text: *The setting, the sentence that never finished, and why the world looks the way it does.*

In ancient history, one person wrote down the **truth of the world** — a record of what was and what is, kept current as the world happened. Then the scribe was **silenced, mid-sentence**. The record simply stops.

Everything before that line has a name, a shape, a settled truth. Everything after it was **never written down** — and what is never written does not hold together. The blank pages that should have carried the rest of the record scattered across the world, and where they landed they **transformed into monsters**: unrecorded space given hostile form.
The world is called *Unwritten* for exactly that reason. Not un-done — **never recorded.** The quest is not to restore a lost book; it is to write the part that was never there.
What the silence did to people

With no record still being kept, **people lost their identities.** Their color, their sense of self — all of it drained away, leaving behind **charcoal-like husks**. A body still stands: present, real, solid. But nobody's name was ever inked.
The husks did not simply give up. They wander a seemingly endless journey across the world, **hunting the scattered pages** — trying to finish what the scribe never got to write. You are one of them.
Nothing about how Unwritten looks is arbitrary. The visual style *is* the story:

items: **The flat, papery monsters are blank pages.** They are literally paper — the pages that should have held the rest of the record and never did. Their flatness isn't an art choice; it's what they are.

**The colorless, charcoal heroes are people who were never named.** The body is 3D and fully present, but no ink ever reached it — no color, no self. A faint trace of identity still clings on: a hint of colored hair, an inked eye.
**What you take from a page is text you put on it.** To defeat a monster is to *fill it in* — one more line of the record that now exists because you wrote it.

blocks.text: Progression in Unwritten is the story of **getting your color.** As a husk writes more of the record — growing stronger, journeying further, uncovering story, mastering a weapon — **color returns to them**, identity leaking in for the first time. A fully realized hero is one who has written a great deal of themselves into existence.

Twelve people fought the thing that silenced the scribe. Because they acted **after** the last written line, none of it was recorded — not the battle, not whether they won. They left **twelve weapons** and no names.

items: **Each of the twelve weapons is one of them.** A weapon is not a tool; it is the only surviving trace of a person the record never captured. How the weapon fights *is* how that person fought.
**They are known only by epithet, never by name** — the Shield is *The One Who Stood*, the Dagger is *The Late Arrival*. The missing name is the point, and it is also the reward.
**A dropped weapon remembers its wielder in fragments.** That is why two of the same weapon can carry different skills: it isn't randomness, it's which memories surfaced this time.
**Carrying one bleeds their identity into you** — this is the charcoal-to-color return. You are not recovering *the* truth; you are finishing *a* story.
**Naming an Unwritten is the endgame.** Learn enough of a weapon's skills and its true name can finally be written down — twelve names to write, twelve journeys to finish.

rows: Met every challenge alone, one at a time, and never lost the exchange.
The One Who Cleared the Road
Walked ahead of the others so there would be a path behind.
Would not be turned, would not defend, only pressed forward.
Whatever the enemy meant to do, it did not get to.
The One Who Moved the Line
Decided where everyone stood, on both sides.
Took what was meant for the other eleven.
Was never where the blow landed, and never out of range.
Was not in the fight until it was already ending.
Needed one shot; waited as long as that took.
The One Who Burned the Field
Unmade the ground the enemy was standing on.
The One Who Brought Them Back
Is the reason the other eleven were still standing.
Did nothing quickly, and nothing survived it.

blocks.text: The great powers of the world

items: **The silencer** — the thing that stopped the scribe mid-sentence, and the deepest blankness in the world.
**Bosses** — larger, self-assembled masses of blank page: absence gathered into something powerful and deliberate.
**The scattered pages** — the ordinary monsters of the world, and the reason to keep walking.
